turn_text: One of the most fundamental debates in international relations is how to maintain peace between competing nation-states. Do governments seek to maximize security or power? Do policies of deterrence or accommodation more effectively secure our interests against our adversaries? Americans must wrestle with these questions because they're bigger than faculty lounge banter. They are the starting point of foreign policy in the foundation of national security. More often than not, you can trace the political disagreements about America's foreign policy that you read in the news back to these basic questions. Whether it's China, Russia, Iran, or the pullout from Afghanistan, the Biden administration is wrestling day in and day out with these calculations. The deterrent side of this debate was perhaps most eloquently articulated by former President Ronald Reagan when he talked about peace through strength and how securing an overwhelming strategic advantage for America makes the world more stable, not less. And for today's episode of the podcast, I have the privilege of interviewing one of America's foremost defenders of the piece through strength approach today, United States Senator Ted Cruz. He has represented Texas in the Senate since 2013, and is a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and previously a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. And on a personal note, he was my boss in the Senate, where I staffed him for five years on Indo-Pacific policy. Senator, it's wonderful to have you on the podcast. Thanks for joining today.

Now, note for a second that prior to that event, almost nobody on earth had ever heard of Darryl Morrie. I know he was because I'm a big rockets fan, but I'd be willing to bet you didn't know who he was. And I'd be willing to bet almost nobody watching this podcast knew who he was. But China reacted screaming in hysteria. And the NBA grovel, LeBron James grovel. By the way, I will say, Edith Cantor, his tennis shoe is taking on LeBron James and showing him bowing down before the Chinese communist government officials. That's been an enormous amount of courage. I'm grateful for Cantor calling out LeBron. The contrast, the Women's Tennis Association has a lot bigger balls than the NBA. And I'd like to see courage extend more broadly. I hope, number one, that China gives in under the pressure and scrutiny and sunlight, and number two, that others have the courage to stand up. Now, you asked about the Olympics also. Listen, there are some who are advocating that America should boycott the Olympics. I'm not one of them. I look back, we talked about Jimmy Carter. Jimmy Carter tried that in the late 70s, and it was a disaster. The American boycott, all it did was hurt American athletes. And there's a whole generation of athletes, young men and young women, who have worked their whole lives preparing for this moment, who have put in tens of thousands of hours of practice. And to simply say to those American athletes, you know, hey, sorry for the last 10, 20 years of your life, but boom, it's gone. I think that's wrong. So I think the boycott is an ineffective tool for standing up to China. Now, let me be clear, I'm not saying that we should go and grovel to China. I think we should go over there, send our athletes over there. I do agree with the concept of a diplomatic boycott not sending our senior officials over there trying to deny the legitimacy and attention. I think our athletes should compete along with the personnel necessary to ensure their security and safety. But I think what is critically important is that we should call out the Chinese atrocities, that we should have courage to call out to go to Beijing and call out the murder, call out the torture, call out the concentration camp, call out the lies, call out the Chinese Communist government's culpability and responsibility for the Wuhan virus and for the cover up and for the lives that have been lost. that we need to call that out unequivocally. And as I said, to Margaret Brennan on face the nation, we need to go over there and kick their commie assets. And by the way, Michael, I will say it was very funny watching Margaret's expression. She was so startled at the idea that we should go and win. But I think that is an embodiment of peace through strength, which is the path forward we should be following.
